messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] Comparative study for ERGM vs its rival models
messages.body_plain:
Hi, Hamid.  The term "exponential family random graph model" refers to a 
way of parameterizing models for networks, not for a "kind" of network 
model in the sense that a scientist would use the term.  Thus, to ask 
for a "competing" model is senseless (rather like asking for sonnets 
that compete with the English language).  In the case of the Kronecker 
graph family, for instance, it is necessarily true that (at least the 
versions I have seen) must have an equivalent exponential family 
expression, though that expression may or may not be parsimonious, 
convenient, intelligible, etc.

In a nutshell, you should think of the ERG form as a formal language for 
describing network models.  Choice of language is driven by many 
considerations, and there are certainly cases in which the exponential 
family representation is cumbersome and unhelpful.  (The inhomogeneous 
Bernoulli graphs come to mind.)  One should not, however, confuse choice 
of language with choice of model.

-Carter

sense to say that (1) reciprocity is stronger in the friendship
network, and (2) reciprocity is 4.5 times stronger in the friendship
network?

Thanks a lot for your help!

Best,
Balazs

random number generator in an effort to make your results *exactly*  
reproducible, then your results probably will have changed anyway from  
version 2.2-2 to 2.2-3.  But again, the change should be small.

Dave

messages.body_plain:
Hi, Sam -

Sam Stewart wrote:
> Do you mean treat the bipartite network as a standard network?  When I 
> run sedist on a 2-mode network I get this:
> 
> Error in d[1, , ] <- dat : 
>   number of items to replace is not a multiple of replacement length
> 
> The error occurs because the sedist function uses as.sociomatrix.sna to 
> extract the sociomatrix, but then it sets up the dissimilarity matrix (d 
> in the sedist code) to be square, using dim(dat)[1], while the 
> sociomatrix is not square.
> 
> If I set up the 2-mode network as a bipartite network, but didn't 
> actually record it as a bipartite network, then the resulting 
> sociomatrix would be 617x617 (rather than 300x317), with large 0 blocks 
> in the top-left and bottom right.  If I were to run a partitioning on 
> that would it be meaningful?

Yes, you will need to represent your matrix in one-mode form (i.e., as a 
bipartite graph on the union of row and column vertices); you can do 
that an adjacency matrix will work fine here, as will an sna edgelist. 
At that point, sedist and friends will operate normally.  Note that the 
meaning of structural equivalence is the same in one-mode and two-mode 
contexts (i.e., v and v' are structurally equivalent to the extent that 
they have identical neighborhoods in V minus v,v'), and analysis 
proceeds as usual.  (You might interpret the block structure 
differently, however, depending on the meaning of the row and column 
vertices.  When using redist, you might also want to begin by 
differentiating between the row and column vertices in the seed partition.)

Hope that helps,

-Carter

messages.body_plain:
Three points:

1. As noted, shrinking plot elements is important with very large 
displays.  You will want to set your vertex.cex to something suitably 
small.  Getting the ideal values for parameters like repulse.rad 
requires some testing in difficult cases; recall that custom coordinates 
can also be specified if needed.

2. R's default plot margins eat a lot of space.  Setting the "mar" 
argument with "par" can help.

3. Semi-transparancy has been supported in gplot/plot.network for as 
long as R has supported it -- it's a standard feature.  (Just pass a 
color with an alpha parameter.)

4. Currently, gplot in sna is slightly more advanced than plot.network. 
  (It lacks some of plot.network's conveniences, however.)

Hope that helps,

-Carter
